subject: Dedicated SKU guidance: headroom vs concurrency for Acme AI commitment
messages:
From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.com>
To: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>
Cc: Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-09-18T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: internal: quick take on Acme sizing before customer call

Folks — prepping for the call with Acme later today. High-level deviation from our standard playbook because their workload mixes very large-context summarization jobs (nightly batch + online preview) and a heavy real-time embedding/QA surface for search. Notes: 

- Workload breakdown (Acme estimate): 30% long-context summarization (window > 32k), 40% high-concurrency autocomplete/QA (short context), 30% embedding/cheap generation.
- Constraint: customer wants a single Dedicated contract for predictability; they’ve signaled willingness to pay for headroom on timeline-sensitive features if we justify it.

My draft recommendation: a mixed pool that emphasizes headroom for the long-context tail while keeping lots of cheap replication for concurrency:
  * H100 (SXM, high-bandwidth) — reserve a small cluster for long-context models and tail-latency sensitive ops; prefer these for 64k-like workloads and KV-heavy caching (approx 3–5 nodes).
  * A100 (40/80GB) — the throughput workhorse for medium-length contexts and batching; good price/perf balance for client’s standard generations (approx 8–12 nodes).
  * L4 (cost-efficient) — serve embeddings, small context chat, and burstable traffic (approx 18–25 nodes).

Operational levers to include in the quote: automatic model fallthrough (H100 -> A100 -> L4), prefix KV caching, and a cross-tier autoscale for predictable burst coverage.

I’ll loop in the cost model (attached) but want to be explicit on two tradeoffs to discuss with Acme: memory headroom vs concurrency. If we bias too much toward H100 we lose tokens-per-dollar for typical interactive traffic; if we bias too much to L4 they’ll hit degradation on long-context jobs.

If you agree with the split above, I’ll propose the concrete numbers and monthly committed nodes to the customer and include a 3-month canary with metrics-based rollback.

— Vivek
From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.com>
To: Sam Turner <sam.turner@acme.ai>
Cc: Acme AI procurement <procurement@acme.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-09-18T13:05:00-07:00
Subject: Proposed Dedicated pool for Acme: balancing headroom and concurrency

Hi Sam — great discussion earlier. Per our conversation, attached is a pragmatic Dedicated pool proposal and the cost workbook. TL;DR recommendation (first-year committed pool):

- 4 x H100 nodes (reserved) — targets the long-context summarization and nightly batch jobs; provides headroom for peak large-context runs and keeps KV-cache residency high.
- 10 x A100 nodes (reserved, mix of 40GB/80GB) — primary throughput capacity for mid-length generation with good batching economics.
- 20 x L4 nodes (reserved) — handle embeddings, cheap chat, and burstable concurrency; these are the most cost-efficient tokens-per-dollar for standard interactive traffic.

Why this mix:
- H100: best tail-latency and large-sequence memory (we recommend H100-backed model variants for >32k context).
- A100: excellent throughput with mature quantization profiles for most open models.
- L4: lowest unit cost for short-context ops, ideal for embeddings and caching-heavy workloads.

We will enable automatic routing so requests are steered by policy (latency-sensitive -> H100; best-cost -> L4) and a fallback plan if H100 slots are saturated. The attached workbook models three scenarios (conservative, expected, optimistic) with token volumes and monthly committed costs.

If this looks reasonable I can convert the numbers into the reserved-capacity proposal and send a DocuSign for the annual commitment. We can also structure an initial 3-month canary with metrics to validate the mix.

Best,
Vivek

Attachments: SKU_cost_model_ACME_v2.xlsx, latency_v_memory_tradeoffs.pdf
From: Sam Turner <sam.turner@acme.ai>
To: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.com>
Cc: Acme AI procurement <procurement@acme.ai>
Date: 2027-09-19T08:21:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Proposed Dedicated pool for Acme: balancing headroom and concurrency

Vivek — thanks for the clear breakdown and workbook. Quick reactions from our side: 

1) The split makes conceptual sense, but 4 H100 nodes feels heavy relative to our budget. Can we reduce H100 to 2 and lean on A100 fallthrough for medium-long jobs?
2) We need to ensure predictable monthly cost — would you recommend smoothing by committing fewer H100 but adding guaranteed burst credits?
3) Also curious how much headroom (in GB of model KV) you’d realistically preserve per H100 node for our 64k summarization jobs. Any ballpark numbers we can use in sizing?

If we can adjust the mix and show a cost/latency tradeoff matrix that keeps our effective monthly spend within the procurement envelope, I think we can move quickly.

— Sam
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
To: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.com>, Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>
Cc: Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-09-20T10:47:00-07:00
Subject: Re: internal: Acme sizing follow-up + cost adjust

Quick ops note and proposed counter:

- Reduce H100 reserved to 2 nodes, add a 12-month burst pool (on-demand H100 capacity credits) that Acme can draw against for large nightly runs. This preserves token economics while granting them headroom when scheduled.
- Increase A100 to 14 reserved nodes (to absorb some long-context via tiling/LLM-quantization fallthrough) and keep L4 at 20 reserved.
- Offer a priced canary: first 3 months we bill on 70% of the committed H100 baseline and allow up to 50% additional burst (metered) at a negotiated unit price. After month 3, re-evaluate based on actual tail utilization and move to full commitment or normalize.

Notes for response to Sam: include a short table showing expected p95 latency and token cost across the three tiers for the three canonical workload types (we can keep it qualitative in the email, quantitative table in the workbook). Also attach SKU_cost_model_ACME_v2.xlsx and mark the scenario that matches the new split.

— Karthik
From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.com>
To: Sam Turner <sam.turner@acme.ai>, Acme AI procurement <procurement@acme.ai>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>, Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-09-22T16:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Proposed Dedicated pool for Acme: updated proposal and next steps

Sam — thanks for the honest feedback. We’ve revised the proposal to strike a balance between guaranteed headroom and monthly cost predictability. Summary of updated commitment: 

- Reserved: 2 x H100, 14 x A100 (mixed 40/80GB), 20 x L4.
- Burst credits: a guaranteed H100 burst pool allowing up to 50% additional H100 capacity during scheduled nightly windows (metered beyond base commitment).
- Billing smoothing: for the first 3 months we bill at 70% of committed H100 baseline and meter any burst usage at a negotiated rate (details in attached workbook, scenario: "Balanced headroom").

Ballpark on KV/residency: with our recommended H100-backed model variants and the KV caching profile we suggest, you should expect enough KV residency per H100 node to comfortably serve multiple concurrent 64k summaries when requests are sharded/tiling is enabled. Exact GBs depend on model variant; we modeled conservative and optimistic residency in the workbook — see the "latency_v_memory_tradeoffs.pdf" appendix for the breakdown.

Next steps: I can convert this into an editable contract and send a DocuSign link. If you'd like, we'll also kick off the 3-month canary with a weekly dashboard and a joint review at week 8.

If this sounds good I’ll get the DocuSign over today.

— Vivek

Attachments: SKU_cost_model_ACME_v2.xlsx, latency_v_memory_tradeoffs.pdf
